museumsArt.label: Museums & Art
museumsArt.about: Museums, galleries and art as a reason to visit: the major collections, the best-known museums, art districts, and recurring shows or fairs.
museumsArt.notCount: Historic sites and architecture (own interests; mention them only where they are also a museum); street life.
museumsArt.scope: Museums, galleries and art as a reason to visit: the major collections, the best-known museums, art districts, and shows or fairs that recur. It applies wherever a visitor can spend meaningful time in museums or galleries, even a small number; it does not apply where there are none worth a visit.

architecture.label: Architecture
architecture.about: Buildings and built places as a reason to visit: notable architecture from any period, skylines, historic and modern districts, bridges, and planned or ruined places seen for their design.
architecture.notCount: What is inside buildings (museums), religious use (Religious & Spiritual Sites), and the history behind a site (History & Archaeology).
architecture.scope: Buildings and built places as a reason to visit: notable architecture from any period (historic, modern, vernacular), skylines, districts, bridges, and planned or ruined places seen for their design. It applies wherever a visitor can see buildings worth traveling for, even a single district or a single landmark.

historyArchaeology.label: History & Archaeology
historyArchaeology.about: Ancient and historic sites, ruins, castles, battlefields, palaces, old towns and the museums that interpret them.
historyArchaeology.notCount: Buildings seen only for their design (Architecture) and places of worship seen as living religious sites (Religious & Spiritual Sites).
historyArchaeology.scope: History and archaeology as a reason to visit: ancient and historic sites, ruins, castles, battlefields, palaces, old towns and the museums that interpret them. It applies wherever a visitor can reach sites with real historical depth; recent history counts when visitors travel to see it.

religiousSites.label: Religious & Spiritual Sites
religiousSites.about: Cathedrals, temples, mosques, shrines, monasteries, pilgrimage routes and sacred places, visited whatever the visitor's own beliefs; what can be seen and done, and the etiquette and access that matter.
religiousSites.notCount: Buildings valued only for design (Architecture) or as ruins and history (History & Archaeology).
religiousSites.scope: Religious and spiritual sites as places to visit, whatever the visitor's own beliefs: cathedrals, temples, mosques, shrines, monasteries, pilgrimage routes and sacred natural places. Cover what visitors can see and do, and the access and etiquette that matter (dress, hours, no entry during services). It applies wherever there are such sites visitors travel for.

traditionalCrafts.label: Traditional Arts & Crafts
traditionalCrafts.about: Workshops, markets and villages where traditional crafts (textiles, ceramics, woodwork, metalwork, glass, paper and the like) are still made, and where a visitor can see them made or buy them.
traditionalCrafts.notCount: Mass-produced souvenirs, general shopping (Shopping), and art museums (Museums & Art).
traditionalCrafts.scope: Traditional arts and crafts as a reason to visit: workshops, markets and villages where traditional crafts are still made, and where a visitor can watch them being made or buy them. It applies only where living craft traditions exist that a visitor can reach; mass-produced souvenirs do not count.

cityExploration.label: Local Culture & City Exploration
cityExploration.about: Getting a feel for a place by exploring it: neighborhoods worth wandering, squares, local markets as street life, daily rhythms and customs.
cityExploration.notCount: Museums, food, nightlife and shopping (own interests).
cityExploration.scope: Exploring a place and getting a feel for everyday local life: neighborhoods worth wandering, squares, street life, daily rhythms and local customs, and how easy and pleasant the place is to explore. It applies wherever there is a town or city a visitor can explore; it does not apply where nobody lives within reach.

fineDining.label: Fine Dining
fineDining.about: Serious restaurants and tasting menus, chef-led cooking and the places known for it.
fineDining.notCount: Casual local eating and markets (Street Food & Markets).
fineDining.scope: Fine dining as a reason to visit: serious restaurants and tasting menus, chef-led cooking and the places known for it, and the local cuisine they build on. It applies wherever a visitor can eat at restaurants of real culinary ambition; it does not apply where there is none within a day trip. Do not name any individual restaurant, chef or hotel: describe the style of cooking and where the scene is concentrated (a city or district). When the fine dining is limited to one city or district that many visitors spend little time in, say so. Where cooking is not a reason to visit, say so plainly and keep the scores low.

streetFood.label: Street Food & Markets
streetFood.about: Food stalls, night markets, food halls, market-led eating and the local specialties people eat on the street.
streetFood.notCount: Sit-down fine dining (Fine Dining) and drinks (Wine, Beer & Spirits; Specialty Coffee & Tea).
streetFood.scope: Street food and markets as a reason to visit: food stalls, night markets, food halls, market-led eating and the local specialties people eat on the street. It applies wherever there is food a visitor can eat at stalls or markets, even a single market. Where the street food is mainly farmers' markets and weekly markets, vendors, crowds and produce thin out in cold or wet months: score it. Market halls and named markets may be named; individual stalls may not.

coffeeTea.label: Specialty Coffee & Tea
coffeeTea.about: Roasters and serious café culture, tea houses and tea ceremonies, and where coffee or tea is grown or traditionally drunk.
coffeeTea.notCount: Chain cafés, and alcohol (Wine, Beer & Spirits).
coffeeTea.scope: Specialty coffee and tea as a reason to visit: roasters and serious café culture, tea houses and ceremonies, and the places where coffee or tea is grown or traditionally drunk. It applies wherever there is a coffee or tea culture a visitor can seek out; chain cafés do not count. Coffee or tea farms and estates count only if a visitor can reach them on a day trip from the place; coffee served at lodges and hotels does not count. Do not name individual cafés or roasters.

wineSpirits.label: Wine, Beer & Spirits
wineSpirits.about: Wine regions and cellar doors, breweries and beer halls, distilleries and traditional local drinks.
wineSpirits.notCount: Bars as nightlife (Nightlife), and imported drinks alone.
wineSpirits.scope: Wine, beer and spirits as a reason to visit: wine regions and cellar doors, breweries and beer halls, distilleries and traditional local drinks. It applies wherever visitors can tour or taste local production or drink at places known for it; imported drinks alone do not count. Beer, cider and spirits count as much as wine: judge the whole scene. Name regions, wine routes and festivals, not individual producers, bars or brewpubs.

scenicLandscapes.label: Scenic Landscapes
scenicLandscapes.about: Natural and rural scenery worth traveling to see: mountains, deserts and canyons, coasts, forests, lakes and waterfalls, glaciers and ice, and the viewpoints and drives that show them.
scenicLandscapes.notCount: The night sky (Stargazing), city architecture (Architecture, City Exploration), wildlife, wildflowers and the northern lights, and photography technique.
scenicLandscapes.scope:
Scenery as a reason to visit: mountains, deserts and canyons, coasts, forests, lakes, rivers and waterfalls, glaciers and ice, and the viewpoints, drives and walks that show them. It applies wherever a visitor can see scenery worth the trip, even modestly; never mark it not applicable. Name parks, viewpoints, passes and routes only when you are sure of them; do not name tour operators or hotels.
How to score the place. The facts give our ratings for each landscape type, each against the best of that type in the world. The best type sets the level of the place; several strong types lift it a little. A 10.0 needs a world-best landscape and a famous signature view; most places never reach it. A place whose only strong rating is cities and villages (flat urban beauty, for example Paris) is capped at about 6.0 here, because city beauty belongs to Architecture and City Exploration. The exception is a city or village whose setting is itself the view (water, a caldera, a fjord, canals, a mountain backdrop): score it by that landscape.
How to score the months. Score how well a visitor can see and reach the scenery, not how comfortable the weather is. A month goes down only for a real reason: access (passes, roads, trails, ferries or lodges closed), visibility (monsoon cloud, fog, smoke), the scenery itself changing (waterfalls at low flow, snow cover that hides or reveals the view, glaciers or ice open only in summer, autumn color), or daylight (a polar winter with a few hours of light). Cold or heat alone does not lower a month unless it blocks the view. Score 0 only when the place cannot be reached at all that month. If nothing real changes, score every month alike.
Do not write about wildflowers, wildlife, the northern lights or stars here; they have their own interests. Scenery is implied, not announced: never write "scenic landscapes" or call a place a destination for scenery; just describe the views. Write the place as the subject of the overview: "Northern Ireland is known for its dramatic coastline", never "Northern Ireland's scenery is known for ..." or "The landscape is known for ..."; when we think of a place we already think of its scenery. Give each overview sentence one subject (the coast, then the interior), not a sentence that lists both ends of the place at once. Name a famous ancient site when it is part of the view (Bagan's temples, Tikal, Teotihuacan). Read each sentence back for sense: nothing on the shore is inland.

stargazing.label: Stargazing
stargazing.about: Dark skies, the Milky Way and the stars: remote and high places with clear nights, certified dark-sky sites and good places to photograph the night sky.
stargazing.notCount: Scenic views by day (Scenic Landscapes), the northern lights (Aurora), and observatories visited as buildings or museums.
stargazing.scope:
Stargazing as a reason to visit: how dark and clear the best night sky a visitor can reach is, and how good it is for seeing the Milky Way and the stars. It applies wherever a visitor can look up at a night sky, even a poor one; for a big city, say plainly that the sky is washed out and name the nearest darker area a day trip away only if you are sure of one. Never mark it not applicable.
Write about the sky in plain words only: never quote hours of darkness, percentages of cloud or the Bortle class, and do not use the word Bortle; say 'very dark', 'mostly clear', 'the sky never gets fully dark'. When darkness is limited by the length of the night, say astronomical darkness and explain it once in plain words (the sun more than 18 degrees below the horizon, so the sky never gets fully dark when twilight lasts all night); "true night" is not a defined term, so do not use it. The length of the night matters only far from the equator. For a place closer to the equator than Seattle (about 47.5 degrees, north or south) never mention the length of the night at all, no "short nights" or "long nights"; lead with what really decides the month (roads closed by snow, cloud and rain). Never mention the moon, moon phases or moonlight: it is the same everywhere on a given night and changes each year, so it is not a fact about a place. Do not write about the northern lights. A meteor shower may be named in its own month (for example the Perseids in August, the Geminids in December) in a few words.
How to score the place. The facts give the Bortle class of the best sky within about two hours' drive of the usual base. Use it for the band: Bortle 1 or 2 scores 8.0 to 10.0; 3 scores 6.5 to 8.0; 4 scores 5.0 to 6.5; 5 scores 3.5 to 5.0; 6 or 7 scores 2.0 to 3.5; 8 or 9 scores under 2.0. Clear high dry skies (thin air, very few cloudy nights), a certified dark-sky site and easy, safe night access move the place up within its band. 10.0 is for the few places a stargazer would name on a world list.
How to score the months, using the facts. 1. Hours of astronomical darkness: a month with 9 or more hours has no penalty; 6 to 9 is a small penalty; 3 to 6 cuts the month by about a third; under 3 cuts it by about two thirds; 0 hours means the sky never gets fully dark, and then the lowest point of the sun at night (in the facts) decides: from -18 to -12 degrees most stars still show (cap the month at about 3.0); from -12 to -9 only the brightest stars and planets show (cap about 1.5); from -9 to -6 a few of the very brightest (cap about 0.5); above -6, including midnight sun, no star shows at all and the month scores exactly 0.0. A few stars and no stars are different months: never put a month with no stars in a blurb with a month where a few show, and never write "if any" for a month that has none; say plainly that the sky never gets dark enough to see a star. In the same way each of these skies gets its own blurb, and a blurb never covers months from two of them: fully dark (the sun below -18); most stars still show (-18 to -12); a few stars show (-12 to -6); no star, with twilight all night (-6 to 0); no star, with the sun up all night (above 0). Where most stars still show, say that twilight lingers and the faintest stars are lost but most stars still show; do not say the sky "never gets fully dark" for such a month, because it sounds like no stars show. The loss of night is not only an Arctic matter: it reaches north of about 48 degrees in summer (most of northern Europe, Canada and southern Patagonia). In polar winter the long darkness helps, but cold or access can still hold the month back. 2. Night cloud: months with night cloud cover above about 60 percent are cut hard, 40 to 60 percent moderately, under about 25 percent are at their best; rainy and monsoon seasons, fog, dust, haze and smoke seasons lower a month too. 3. The Milky Way's bright core is above the horizon at some point in the night from about March to October (well placed through the evening and night from June to August in the northern hemisphere, and from May to August in the southern), and it is not up at night from about November to January except near the equator. Give the months when the core is well placed a small bump of 0.5 to 1.0 where the sky is dark enough to see it, and nothing near the poles or where the sky never gets fully dark. Mention the Milky Way only as its bright core being well placed that month or not up at night; never say when in the evening or night it can be seen. 4. Access: a high road or pass that is closed in winter lowers the month, or zero if the sites cannot be reached. Cold is not a penalty, because the traveler's own comfort setting handles it. If nothing real changes through the year, one blurb and a flat score.

sunbathing.label: Sunbathing
sunbathing.about: Lying in the sun: beaches, resort pool days and lakeshores, in reliably warm, sunny weather.
sunbathing.notCount: Swimming, snorkeling and beach quality as a place to swim (Beaches & Swimming), natural hot springs (Hot Springs), and spas (Spa & Wellness).
sunbathing.scope:
Sunbathing as a reason to visit: warm, sunny days with somewhere good to lie out, whether sand and sea, a resort pool day or a lake or river shore. It applies wherever a visitor can lie in the sun in at least one season; never mark it not applicable, but give a cold or gray place low scores.
How to score the place. The best of three things sets the level: sand and sea, resort pool days, or a lake or river shore. 10.0 is only for the best sand-and-sea places. A place whose sun days are mostly resort pools with no real beach (an inland resort town or desert city) tops out between 8.5 and 9.0, with 9.0 only for the very best pool destinations. The facts give our ratings for beach clubs, quiet shores, resort pool days and calm shores.
How to score the months, using the facts. Temperature, one smooth scale for every place (never a cliff at one number): afternoon highs of about 77 to 95 degrees F are best; 68 is about half the place's peak; 60 is about 1.0 to 1.5; 55 about 0.5; at or below 50 the month is 0, however sunny. Move smoothly between these points, so 66 degrees with sun scores clearly higher than 56 degrees. Above about 100 degrees F lowers a month, but a place with strong resort pool days keeps a floor of 2.0 to 3.0 in its hottest months, never 0, because pool days continue; a beach place is lowered modestly in extreme heat. Rain and cloud: use the sunshine hours and rainy days in the facts; wet and monsoon seasons lower a month. Wind (the calm-shores rating), seaweed seasons and hurricane or cyclone season also lower a month. Do not score crowds, and do not score sea temperature or swimming hazards, which belong to Beaches & Swimming. Sunbathing is a light, casual pleasure, not a sport: never write the word sunbathing, sunbathe or sunbather, and do not call a place a destination for it or build a verdict on the name ("too cold for sunbathing"); describe the sun, the heat, the pools and the beaches and let the reader infer the rest. If nothing real changes through the year, one blurb and a flat score.

spaWellness.label: Spa & Wellness
spaWellness.about: Day spas and massage, thermal baths and hammams, wellness resorts and clinical or cure-style wellness.
spaWellness.notCount: Natural hot springs (Hot Springs), yoga and meditation retreats (Yoga & Wellness Retreats), and luxury hotels in general (Luxury Hotels).
spaWellness.scope:
Spa and wellness as a reason to visit: day spas and massage, thermal baths and hammams, wellness resorts, and clinical or cure-style wellness. It applies wherever a visitor can book a spa treatment or bathe in a built bathing tradition; never mark it not applicable, but give a place with little low scores. Name spa towns, districts and bathing traditions (hammam, onsen, thermal baths); do not name individual spas, hotels or chains.
How to score the place. The facts give our ratings for the four kinds. The strongest one sets the level, not the average: a world-best thermal bath culture makes a place a destination even if its resorts are modest. A place weak in all four scores 2.0 to 4.0. 10.0 is only for the places a wellness traveler would name on a world list.
How to score the months. Spas are indoors, so scores stay close to flat; heat, cold and crowds do not make a month worse. Move a month by at most about 1.5 points, and only for a real reason: outdoor hot-water soaking (Iceland, Japan, Budapest) is better in the cold months; seasonal spa hotels that close in the off season (Alpine and seaside resorts) lower those months only when a large share is shut; Dead Sea-type therapy is poor in extreme summer heat. If bathing or sauna customs here differ from what a traveler would expect (saunas that are mixed-gender and nude in Switzerland, Germany and Austria; swimsuit-only pools; segregated hours), say so once in your own words. In the overview cover all three kinds that exist: day spas and massage, bathing culture (thermal baths, hammam, onsen, jjimjilbang), and wellness retreats or spa hotels; do not let one kind crowd out the others. Natural hot springs are their own interest (Hot Springs): mention them briefly if they are part of the local bathing culture, but do not lead with them. Most places get one blurb for the year and a flat score.
